subject: Re: Performance SLO & Autoscale follow-up (p95 latency, burst capacity)
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Sara Turner <sara.turner@acme.ai>, Tom Li <tom.li@acme.ai>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:15:00 -0700
Subject: Performance SLO & Autoscale follow-up (p95 latency, burst capacity)

Hi Sara / Tom —

Thanks again for a productive call earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment on performance requirements and what Redwood will validate during the technical trial:

1) SLO targets:
- p95 latency: 100ms for short-form streaming responses (<= 512 tokens)
- p99 latency: 300ms target for non-streaming batch generation
- Throughput: baseline 120 qps steady-state, burst to 600 qps for 3–5 minute windows
- Concurrency per model replica: expected 12 concurrent streams average

2) Streaming requirements:
- Streaming with token-by-token flush required for UI responsiveness (client-side consumption).
- Need max initial token time (TTI) under 60ms for first partial chunk.

3) Autoscaling & burst behavior:
- Warm pool of pre-warmed workers to cover immediate 200 qps of burst with <5s ramp for that portion.
- Cold scale-up path for additional capacity estimated at ~90–120s to provision new GPU-backed workers (depends on instance type).
- Queueing/backpressure: Redwood supports short queueing with progressive degradation; we recommend client-side queue length limit + graceful 429s when queue hits safe threshold.

4) Data points Redwood will provide during trial:
- Per-route p50/p95/p99 latency histograms, token-level cost, concurrency heatmaps, and warm-pool utilization metrics.
- Traces for any requests that exceed SLOs.

Next steps:
- I attached a one-page SLO_requirements_v1.pdf and an autoscale-diagram.png that maps warm pool vs. cold scaling.
- Please confirm the p95/p99 numbers above and any adjustments to burst window or concurrency expectations.
- If agreed, we'll provision a 2-week technical trial with dedicated capacity to validate these numbers and follow with a performance report.

Action items:
- Sara: confirm SLOs & peak burst windows by EOD Mon (08/16).
- Marissa: provision trial config and share onboarding checklist; will loop in infra engineer Jonas.

Thanks — talk soon.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com

Thanks Marissa — that recap looks great and mirrors our notes. A few clarifications from our side:

- p95 100ms (streaming) is tight but doable for short responses; we can tolerate p95 up to 150ms if it reduces cost significantly. Could you include a cost/latency tradeoff for 100ms vs 150ms in the trial report?
- Burst windows: our product can have sudden traffic from 0 to ~500 qps for 2–4 minutes on promotional pushes. The 600 qps allowance is fine but we should validate the 0->burst ramp path.
- Warm pool: what are the memory/instance sizing recommendations to keep KV cache hits high for context sizes up to 4k tokens?

Also looping in Tom to confirm the integration points for streaming websocket fallback and whether Redwood's streaming can handle our client ACK signals.

We'll confirm final SLOs by EOD Monday — tentatively: p95=125ms (streaming), baseline 100 qps, burst 500 qps.

Thanks,
Sara
Director of Product — Acme AI

Subject: Re: Performance SLO & Autoscale follow-up (p95 latency, burst capacity)

Sara — perfect, thanks for the tentative numbers. A few notes on the technical details you asked about and proposed trial plan:

- Cost/latency tradeoff: we'll run two parallel configs in the trial: (A) lower-latency (aim p95=100ms) with more reserved warm capacity and smaller batching windows; (B) cost-optimized (aim p95=150ms) with slightly higher batching to improve throughput. We'll include per-token cost estimates in the post-trial report.
- Warm pool sizing & KV cache: for 4k token contexts we recommend 1.5–2x memory headroom per worker. We'll provide recommended instance types and quantization profiles in the onboarding doc. Warm pool will keep a digest of hot model weights and recent KV caches for pinned customer models to improve cold-start quality.
- Streaming & client ACKs: Redwood's streaming supports backpressure and client ACK signals; we can surface token acknowledgements to your websocket layer so you can throttle or drop. We'll confirm throughput with Tom during the onboarding call.
- Scale-up times: based on our Dedicated region profiles, cold scale to new GPU workers typically falls in the 90–120s range. For your bursts, warm pool provisioning (pre-warmed) covers immediate surge up to its capacity (<5s ramp), after which additional cold scale is expected.

Proposed trial config & timing:
- Trial duration: 14 days starting once we get your confirmation and a test API key.
- Config: reserved warm pool to cover 200 qps, autoscale min=4 replicas, max=80 (subject to instance selection); two test scenarios (steady-state + promotional burst).
- Deliverables: daily SLO dashboards, final performance report with cost/latency comparison and recommendations.

Jonas / Dev — can you confirm the warm-pool instance types and provide a short list of recommended instance sizes for 4k contexts? If possible, include an estimate of memory headroom and expected KV cache hit ratio assumptions.

Sara — once we lock on instance types I'll create the onboarding checklist and provision the trial.

Best,
Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Marissa / Dev — quick internal note and numbers I pulled from our recent benchmarks to share with Acme during the trial:

- Recommended instance family for 4k contexts: rtx-a6000-like (48 GB) or equivalent multi-GPU partitioning. Expect ~1.6–1.9x memory headroom at default kv-cache sizes.
- Warm-pool sizing: recommend pre-warmed pool to cover 200 qps (as proposed). With the instance types above, that maps to ~6–8 pre-warmed workers depending on model size and token length assumptions.
- KV cache hit ratio assumptions: for sticky traffic patterns we see 65–80% hit rate with a 24-hour warm pool; lower for highly diverse prompts. We'll surface per-route cache hit heatmaps in the trial dashboards.
- Scale-up measured median time-to-ready for new workers (image spin + init): 95s on average in our US Gov Dedicated cluster; 110s in cold public cloud regions.
- Queueing behavior: by default we enforce a soft queue that holds up to 250ms extra latency before returning 429s; we can tune this threshold per route.

I'll draft a short appendix for the trial doc summarizing these numbers and drop it into the shared Drive link.

Jonas Weber
Infra Lead — Redwood Inference
jonas.weber@redwood.com
